extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of natural philosophy / physics; readers interested in metrology and principles of measurement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for designing, using, calibrating, and selecting instruments and units of measurement (time, space, mass, heat, etc.), and for assessing attainable accuracy. Emphasises comparison, standards, systematic procedure, and limits of different standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument as means of comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: A measuring instrument serves and should serve only as a means of comparison between two or more magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat divisions of scales as arbitrary marks and determine their values by comparison with the standard itself. Examples: perpendicular wires in transit telescopes are fixed then their angular intervals are determined by watching star passages and noting clock intervals; the angular value of each micrometer screw turn is ascertained by comparison. Do not attempt to make scale divisions exact multiples of the unit by construction alone; calibrate by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration by reference to known standards (thermopile/galvanometer example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When instrument-scale values cannot be calculated a priori, measure them by placing the instrument before a body of known dimensions, distance, temperature, and radiating power to obtain a known amount of radiation and thus determine the instrument's indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: thermopile calibrated by known radiator; Joule's method of determining temperature produced by compression by matching galvanometer deflection produced by thermopile dip into waters of known temperature. When a carefully constructed instrument (e.g., standard barometer/thermometer) is accepted as a standard, treat inferior instruments comparatively and determine their scales by comparison with the assumed standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicacy by multiplication in apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme delicacy of a measurement method may result from multiplication of effect at several points in the apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include increasing number of thermopile elements or junctions; multiplying galvanometer current effect by passing current many times round a coil; increasing needle excursions by rendering it astatic and improving suspension; observing angular divergence via attached mirror and distant scale with a telescope. Example: Dr. Joule's thermopile indicating 0.000014 Cent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect measurement by conversion of quantity (time↔angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute intervals of one kind (e.g., time) can be estimated by transforming them into another measurable quantity (e.g., angular deviation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Wheatstone/Foucault revolving mirror: duration of electric spark inferred from apparent elongation due to rapidly rotating mirror; Foucault used rotating mirror to measure time taken by light to traverse a few metres. This illustrates using indirect physical transduction to access otherwise unmeasurable small quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic performance: reference determinations and hierarchical comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: When a large number of accurate measurements are needed, make a certain number with scrupulous care and use them as points of reference for remaining determinations; use hierarchical triangulation or standard tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: trigonometrical survey uses principal triangulation fixing a few points with rigid accuracy and a minor triangulation referring other points to these; astronomical surveys use tables of standard stars (Greenwich). For specific gravities, refer gases to atmospheric air and liquids/solids to water. Procedure: determine some anchor/reference values accurately, then relate other measurements to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intermediate comparisons for very large/small ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing a very great with a very small magnitude, break the process into several steps using intermediate terms of comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt direct comparison across huge ratios. Examples: measure London–Edinburgh via a surveyed base rather than laying rods the whole way; compare sun and star brightness by using the full moon as an intermediate unit (Wollaston and Herschel's chain of ratios).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of repetition to improve accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of measurements is a general method to reduce error and improve accuracy where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly referenced as a principal advantage of the pendulum and of weight determinations: repeated weighings can approach very small relative errors. Use repetition plus careful reference determinations as part of systematic measurement practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendulum as a premier measuring instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The pendulum is by far the most perfect and beautiful instrument of measurement: simple in construction, applicable to repetition, and connecting space, time, and force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For small oscillations the square of the time of oscillation is proportional to the length and inversely proportional to the force affecting it (Huygens' formula). Uses: astronomical clocks (time measurement), torsion pendulums to determine Earth's density, determination of variation of gravity, measurements in electricity and magnetism via vibrations. Ensure conditions for small oscillations and constancy of suspension and pendulum properties when using.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of pendulum as an absolute standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Although excellent for subdivision and for many measurements, the pendulum fails as an ultimate standard because slightest changes (form, weight, corrosion, suspension) falsify results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperature, friction, resistance, and minute physical changes affect pendulum properties. Therefore it cannot be relied upon as an invariable long-term standard of time or length without careful control/correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attainable accuracy expectations by quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Different physical magnitudes have different practically attainable accuracies; few measurements exceed six significant figures; time is generally most exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative figures: Sir George Airy estimated time to one part in 8,640,000; mean solar vs sidereal day known to ~1e-8; good balances ≈1 part in 500,000, Stas's balance 1/825,000, some balances reach ~1e6; typical length determinations in base lines ≈1/60,000, exceptional surveys (Cape Comorin) ~1/1,382,400; Whitworth's touch method detects changes ~1e-6 inch. Use these as practical benchmarks and discriminate between new instrument performance and continuous-use performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a concrete standard unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruments are means of comparison; to express absolute magnitudes we must assume some one arbitrary concrete magnitude (an actual object) as standard; if lost, absolute meaning is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concrete standard is arbitrary in theory and selected for practical convenience. All physical quantities (time, space, density, mass, energy, etc.) must be referred to some concrete standard. Recognise that certain magnitudes (number, angular magnitude) have natural units and are exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural units: number and angular magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of magnitude do not need arbitrary concrete units: (1) abstract number, which needs no special unit; (2) angular magnitude, which has a natural unit in the whole revolution (perigon) or the radian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Angular unit in analysis is chosen so that arc length equals radius (radian ~57°17'44".8). While other fractions of revolution may be used, the geometrical/radian unit simplifies mathematical analysis. These cases contrast with arbitrary choices required for other magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of time standard: astronomical bodies vs physical artefacts vs light-based units
rubrics_metrics.description: Several candidate standards for time: Earth's rotation (astronomical), pendulums/metallic springs/gases (physical artefacts), or undulations of light (suggested as most universal). Each has limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earth's rotation is convenient but not absolutely invariable (tidal friction, cooling, perturbations). Pendulums are susceptible to small physical changes (corrosion, suspension). Proposals: Thomson & Tait suggest metallic spring sealed in vacuum; hydrogen gas elasticity suggested as more constant; Maxwell proposed undulations of light in vacuo as the most universal standard (unit of time tied to vibration whose wavelength is unit of length). Consider long-term stability, observability, and susceptibility to perturbation when choosing a time standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to define/perpetuate unit of length and the single-object principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Three proposed modes to perpetuate a standard length: (1) construct an actual specimen bar, (2) assume the globe as ultimate standard and use a submultiple of some globe dimension, (3) adopt the length of the seconds pendulum. Important principle: the standard length must be defined by one single object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing two 'equal' copies is impossible in absolute terms; if two copies are declared equally correct, future discrepancy causes dispute. If a truly invariable single bar could be preserved, it would avoid such inconvenience. When selecting a method, weigh practical perpetuation, possibility of unique reference, and susceptibility to change.
